description: This project explores abandoned or inactive spacecraft, rovers, and equipment on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Using NASA data, images, and research, it highlights their missions, scientific contributions, current status, and the challenges of operating in extreme space environments. The goal is to present space exploration history and engineering achievements in a simple, engaging way for students and space enthusiasts.
summary: Space Relics is an interactive educational website that explores the stories of human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. It presents four fascinating examples of space exploration hardware, explaining their engineering purpose, role in different missions, and why they remained on other worlds. Through interactive storytelling, search and destination-based filters, the project helps students and space enthusiasts understand the engineering behind space exploration and the legacy of past missions.
details: Space Relics: The Stories Left Behind is an interactive, educational web-based project developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the challenge "Abandoned but Not Forgotten." The project explores four examples of human-made equipment left on the Moon and Mars: 1. Apollo Lunar Module Descent Stage – The lower section of the Lunar Module that helped astronauts land on the Moon. 2. Lunar Roving Vehicle – The battery-powered vehicle that extended astronauts' exploration range during the Apollo missions. 3. Mars Pathfinder Backshell and Parachute – Landing equipment that helped protect and slow the Pathfinder spacecraft during its entry and landing on Mars. 4. Perseverance's Backshell and Parachute – Components of the landing system that helped deliver the Perseverance rover safely to Mars. The website provides an interactive archive where visitors can search for objects, filter stories by destination (Moon or Mars), and explore detailed explanations of each object's engineering purpose, mission role, and reason for remaining behind. It also presents a simple "Deliver, Separate, Remember" concept explaining how spacecraft equipment performs specific mission functions and becomes part of the exploration history. The project is designed for students, educators, and space enthusiasts. It aims to make space exploration history more accessible, demonstrate the engineering behind planetary missions, and encourage interest in aerospace engineering. Technologies Used: - HTML - CSS - JavaScript - GitHub for source-code management and hosting NASA-hosted images, mission histories, and official NASA resources are used for educational reference and verification. This project is an independent educational website prototype and is not an official NASA website or endorsed by NASA.
